title: Final Parking Space: Half-Million-Mile 1990 Honda Civic Wagon

body_markdown:
Tall wagons based on subcompact car platforms sold very well in Japan during the 1980s and well into the following decade, and several Japanese manufacturers offered versions of these vehicles in North America before demand was swept away by the SUV craze. Here’s an example of Honda’s Civic-derived wagon/van/MPV, found in[a Denver-area junkyard](https://coloradoautoandparts.com/#navigation) with an impressive final odometer reading.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Yes, a mere 14,478.6 miles short of traveling a half-million miles. That’s more than 20 times around the Earth at the equator, or to the Moon and back and then some. The average number of miles traversed per year comes to just under 13,500.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Back in June, we saw[a 1993 Civic sedan with 414,982 miles on the clock](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-400k-mile-1993-honda-civic-lx-sedan/) , in the same boneyard as today’s Civic. These days, a discarded Honda or Toyota needs *at least* 400,000 miles to grab my attention; I see dozens of Accords and Camrys with mid-300K final odometer readings during[my junkyard travels](https://www.murileemartin.com/JunkyardGalleryHome.html) each year.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The highest-mile junkyard Honda product I’ve documented was[this 1988 Accord LXi three-door liftback with 626,476 miles](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/classic-cars/a40876508/1988-honda-accord-sets-all-time-high-junkyard-treasure-odometer-record/) . If these cars hadn’t been so rust-prone, I’d have found many more with this kind of mileage. At this moment, the top three places in the[Murilee Martin Junkyard Odometer Standings](https://www.murileemartin.com/Junkyard/JunkyardGallery-300kMileCars.html) are occupied by Toyota and Volvo:[a 1996 Avalon](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/a60580723/1996-toyota-avalon-with-nearly-a-million-miles-is-junkyard-treasure/) ,[a 1985 Camry](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/a61456480/1985-toyota-camry-with-648k-miles-is-junkyard-treasure-in-california/) , and[a 1990 240](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/classic-cars/a41645618/volvo-beats-honda-for-all-time-junkyard-treasure-odometer-record/) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


It was corrosion that finally did today’s FPS subject in. Rust isn’t much of a problem in Front Range Colorado, thanks to single-digit humidity and sparing use of road salt, but this car began its career in a rustier place.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


It was sold new at[Brad Barker Honda](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lJO8UP8Ddao) in Bloomington, Illinois. Barker retired in 2019, and his dealership is now[O’Brien Honda](https://www.obrienteamhonda.com/) .


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Like most extreme-high-mile vehicles I find in their final parking places, the interior in this one is in decent condition.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The kind of owner who does all maintenance and repairs when needed also tends to refrain from trashing a car’s interior. I’ve seen just[a few](https://www.autoblog.com/news/junkyard-gem-1993-honda-civic-vx-hatchback/) 300K-plus-mile cars[with abused interiors](https://www.autoblog.com/features/junkyard-gem-1986-nissan-200sx-with-300k-hard-miles/) during my junkyard travels.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The exterior would look pretty good if not for the rust. I’d wager that this car got retired only when the rot on a critical suspension or chassis component finally got too dangerous.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


If original, this engine is a 1.5-liter SOHC four-cylinder rated at 92 horsepower and 89 pound-feet.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The vacuum hose diagrams on the PGM-FI Hondas of this era are beautifully uncomplicated.


American Honda Motor Company


I make that observation because I suffered for years trying to get mid-1980s CVCC Hondas to pass California emissions testing. These cars featured the notorious “Map of the Universe” vacuum-hose diagram (mercifully, Honda printed identification numbers on each of the vacuum hoses).


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


The transmission is the base five-speed manual. Note how the shift pattern diagram has been nearly erased by millions of gear changes.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


Honda had been building Civics in Ohio for a few years by the time this car was assembled, but all fourth-gen Civic Wagons were built at[the Suzuka factory in Japan](https://global.honda/en/about/group/suzuka.html) .


American Honda Motor Company


Honda sold Civic wagons in the United States for the 1976 through 1991 model years, from the first through fourth generations of the vehicle that made most Americans realize that Soichiro Honda’s company didn’t just[build motorcycles](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ck9wBHW2160) (yes, Honda offered four-wheeled vehicles here well before the Civic first reached our shores as a 1973 model, but even[the N360/Z360](https://murileemartin.substack.com/p/reconstituted-junkyard-jewel-1971) was considered something of an oddity here).


Through 1983, the Civic Wagon looked much like the other subcompact wagons being shipped over by Honda’s Japanese rivals.


American Honda Motor Company


The MPV revolution hit Japan hard during the early 1980s, and Honda joined in with the third-generation Civic. Debuting here as a 1984 model, the new Civic Wagon had the same tall roof, short snout, and angular lines seen on its rivals from Toyota, Nissan and Mitsubishi.


Chrysler Corporation


These little MPVs straddled the van/wagon divide, and in most cases they were considered completely separate models in Japan. For example, the Dodge/Plymouth Colt Vista was sold as the Mitsubishi Chariot in its homeland.


JDM Chariot commercials are worth watching.


Toyota sold its Sprinter Carib as[the Tercel Wagon](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/final-parking-space/final-parking-space-1986-toyota-tercel-sr5-4wd-wagon/) in the United States for the 1983-1988 model years. It was available with front- and four-wheel drive here.


The Nissan Prairie became the Stanza Wagon on our side of the Pacific. Its sliding doors made it more of a minivan than a wagon, which likely stole sales from[the North American version of the Nissan Vanette](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/classic-cars/a1851731/junkyard-treasure-1987-nissan-van-gxe/) (nearly all of which were[recalled and crushed](https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-02-04-fi-19061-story.html) thanks to engine fires).


1990 Honda Civic 4WD Wagon.


American Honda Motor Company


In Japan (and much of the rest of the world), this vehicle was known as the Shuttle. A commercial version called the Pro was sold in Japan through 1996.


American Honda Motor Company


Honda used the Wagovan name only on base-model 1984-1989 Civic Wagons in the United States, but now most American Civic enthusiasts (including me)[apply the name to all of these vehicles](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/the-nearly-forgotten-civic-wagovan-might-be-hondas-path-to-the-future/) regardless of what they were called when new. What Honda called “Real Time 4WD” (and[what we’d call all -wheel-drive](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/what-you-need-to-know-about-awd-vs-4wd/) today) first appeared here on 1987 Civic Wagons; for 1984-1986, regular four-wheel-drive was optional.


[Murilee Martin](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/mmartin/)


If you want to yell at me for *not* calling this car a Wagovan in the article title, go ahead… but keep in mind that I try to use whatever designation the manufacturer applied when the vehicle was new when I write headlines. The photo above is from[a genuine 1988 Wagovan](https://www.autoweek.com/car-life/classic-cars/a40608044/1988-honda-civic-wagovan-is-junkyard-treasure/) .


What replaced the Civic Wagon in North America after 1991? Maybe the Accord Wagon, which was sold here for the 1991 through 1996 model years and then shoved aside by the (Accord-based) Odyssey minivan. The CR-V, which debuted here as a 1997 model, is Civic-derived and has no sliding doors, making it seem like the closest direct descendant of the Wagovan.


Honda pushed the AWD versions in its TV commercials.


You need to go back to the 1984-1987 Civic Wagon commercials to find ones that don’t emphasize snow/off-road prowess.
